threatModel.summary: Jubarte is an in-process Rust DOCX comparison, editing, inspection, revision-resolution and PDF/PNG rendering engine exposed through a native CLI, PyO3 Python bindings/facade, wasm-bindgen browser/Node bindings, Python and Node CLI adapters, and an optional Python MCP stdio server (README.md:12-40; src/lib.rs:15-35; jubarte-python/python/jubarte_redlines/mcp_server.py:373-381). Normal document processing accepts package bytes and returns transformed bytes or reports; host adapters supply filesystem authority. Package admission and checked XML APIs form the principal untrusted-document boundary. Native rendering additionally reads installed fonts and maintains an ambient font index. Conditional privileged workflows are explicit CLI self-update and maintainer release publication. No deployment/user context or authoritative knowledge base was supplied; this is a source-backed architecture map, not completed vulnerability-audit coverage.
assets: Confidential document contents, comments, tracked changes, embedded media, generated PDF/PNG, edit reports and patches; MCP callers receive document text and reports over stdio and output files under their granted root (jubarte-python/python/jubarte_redlines/mcp_server.py:131-150,185-217,245-255).

Integrity of original documents, selected output files, edit targets and source snapshots. Optional source_sha256 binds a semantic edit plan to exact source bytes; schema and anchor checks reject invalid edits (src/edit.rs:1735-1761,2073-2094).

Host process memory/CPU availability against attacker-supplied ZIP/XML/media/font content; normal default and comparison admission budgets differ materially (src/admission.rs:39-100; SECURITY.md:38-74).

Filesystem authority of the local CLI user versus the directory capability granted to an MCP server. Native CLI publication uses ambient authorized paths; MCP reads/publication use an open cap-std directory (src/publication.rs:146-225; jubarte-python/src/lib.rs:1244-1278).

Installed executable integrity, GitHub release assets/checksums, optional release-signing private key, registry publication identities and generated npm/wheel/crate artifacts (src/update.rs:25-48,198-210; .github/workflows/release.yml:252-321,356-369; scripts/release.sh:872-899,919-959,1069).

Ambient font metadata and source paths in the native renderer's font-index.tsv; cached entries cause direct reads of recorded face paths after metadata stamp checks (src/convert/font.rs:3090-3107,3154-3189,3213-3229).
trustBoundaries: Untrusted DOCX bytes enter Rust processing through byte APIs and bindings. Admission limits compressed size, entry count, per-part/aggregate inflation, XML nesting and tag policy; no archive extraction, macro execution or external-reference resolution is intended (src/admission.rs:13-28,63-100; src/document_comparer.rs:6530-6567; src/xmllinq/parse.rs:19-36).

Archive metadata crosses into package interpretation. Normal open_archive invokes zip_defects and refuses inconsistent headers, overlapping/extending entries and unsupported entry types; the deliberately unchecked debug opener is a distinct maintainer inspection path (src/opc/archive.rs:15-51).

Raw XML callers may choose permissive parse_xdocument, which explicitly does not enforce input policy. Checked parsing or prior admission is the caller's responsibility; parsing must not be modeled as uniformly guarded (src/xmllinq/parse.rs:19-36,84-98; SECURITY.md:54-65).

An edit-plan producer controls operations, replacement content and optional snapshot guard. Source hash validation is conditional on source_sha256 being present; semantic edits return memory results before host publication (src/edit.rs:1735-1761,2081-2089).

An MCP client controls tool names, document paths, output paths, plans, rendering options and overwrite flags through a stdio connection. Every registered caller shares the configured directory authority; annotation hints are metadata rather than per-caller authorization. Root is --root or current directory, opened once through _OutputRoot. Python resolution is an early diagnostic; actual reads and writes use the capability (jubarte-python/python/jubarte_redlines/mcp_server.py:54-55,67-108,373-381; jubarte-python/src/lib.rs:1244-1278; src/publication.rs:146-200).

MCP document I/O and local CLI publication have independently enforced authority. OutputRoot validates portable relative paths and rejects output symlinks; publish_paths grants ambient local access. Publication stages every file first but commits per file, so a commit/durability failure can expose a reported partial set. Windows parent-directory sync is explicitly a no-op (src/publication.rs:83-143,168-225,228-273,387-405,431-480).

Python and Node CLI adapters own ambient file access and do not inherit MCP confinement or native publication controls. Their general write helpers directly write destinations after adapter checks (jubarte-python/python/jubarte_redlines/__main__.py:101-133; jubarte-wasm/cli/bin/jubarte-redlines.mjs:52-79,106-111).

Native rendering crosses into ambient font files and persistent font-index state, independently of document publication authority. JUBARTE_FONT_DIR overrides the platform font directory; JUBARTE_FONT_INDEX overrides or disables the index, otherwise the index is in the font directory's parent. Document family names used in cloud-font paths are restricted to one normal path component (src/convert/font.rs:2225-2236,2633-2652,3098-3107,3154-3169,3213-3229).

Explicit self-update grants downloaded release code authority to replace the running executable. Repository/target/archive member and SHA256SUMS.txt are configured in code, a prompt or --yes gates installation, and a regular-file hook validates the extracted binary. Current compiled keys are empty and FIRST_SIGNED_RELEASE is None, so signature enforcement is currently inactive (src/update.rs:25-48,91-109,120-125,198-210,234-257).

Tag pushes trigger build jobs with contents:read, then a contents:write release job publishes dist/* using GITHUB_TOKEN. Optional ZIPSIGN_PRIVATE_KEY reaches the signing step and temporary decoded key files; signatures precede checksums. The local release script separately uses operator registry identities and verifies artifact provenance against the tag (.github/workflows/release.yml:15-21,51-89,230-239,252-321,356-369; scripts/release.sh:872-899,919-959,1069).
attackerCapabilities: A document supplier can control DOCX ZIP records, XML, embedded media/fonts, relationships, revision/comment text and document font family names before a user or embedding service processes the document. They do not thereby control host environment variables, installed fonts, MCP startup root or release accounts (SECURITY.md:38-74; src/admission.rs:13-28; src/convert/font.rs:2225-2236).

An authorized MCP client can invoke all registered tools and select files within the server's granted root, including overwrite=true. Root-wide access is the provided capability; no separate tenants, document ownership identities or per-tool authorization layer is established by this adapter (jubarte-python/python/jubarte_redlines/mcp_server.py:54-108,152-168,373-381).

A less-trusted producer can supply edit JSON and anchored replacement content to a trusted caller. A failure could corrupt document edits or bypass snapshot/anchor invariants; source_sha256 is optional, and the model must not assume it always exists (src/edit.rs:106,1735-1761,2081-2089).

A local actor who can modify shared output directories, font directories or font-index state has a materially different starting capability from a document-only attacker. Assess filesystem races and ambient font-cache integrity only with that prerequisite; do not assume document content controls these locations (src/publication.rs:146-148,431-480; src/convert/font.rs:3154-3189,3213-3229).

An attacker controlling GitHub release assets could alter an archive and adjacent checksum in the current checksum-only updater trust model; this requires release-asset control and an operator invoking installation, rather than ordinary document processing. Documentation explicitly distinguishes corruption detection from independent authenticity (src/update.rs:44-48,245-256; docs/SELF_UPDATE.md:59-80).

A contributor can propose repository/workflow changes, but no supplied context establishes tag-push rights, protected-branch bypass, registry credentials, release-signing keys or production deployment access. Privileged release impact needs that additional authorization or a separately demonstrated crossing (.github/workflows/release.yml:15-21,230-235,261-264,356-369).
securityObjectives: Refuse malformed or resource-excessive untrusted packages before uncontrolled inflation/DOM construction; preserve active configured limits across consumers. Defaults are 64 MiB compressed/per-part, 256 MiB aggregate, 10,000 entries and XML depth 256; comparison defaults are 512 MiB compressed/per-part and 2 GiB aggregate with the same entry/depth caps. Tag defaults include 1,024 attributes, 1,024-byte attribute names, 64 MiB attribute values and 128 MiB start tags (src/admission.rs:63-100; src/xmllinq/parse.rs:48-57).

Keep document relationship targets as data during processing, avoid macro execution and archive extraction, and ensure normal readers interpret ZIP identity/content consistently (src/admission.rs:13-22; src/opc/archive.rs:34-51).

Preserve semantic edit atomicity: reject invalid plans/anchors before returning results, validate a supplied source hash, and distinguish this in-memory guarantee from host filesystem transaction behavior (src/edit.rs:1735-1761,2081-2089; src/publication.rs:83-143).

Confine MCP document reads/writes to its caller-granted directory capability, reject unsafe export names, require overwrite authorization for existing outputs, and report partial publication/durability outcomes accurately (jubarte-python/python/jubarte_redlines/mcp_server.py:67-108; src/publication.rs:146-200,228-273,431-480).

Bind self-update to the intended repository, platform, archive member and selected release, check its checksum, and enforce signatures when compiled policy enables them. Do not represent current checksum-only policy as independent release authenticity (src/update.rs:25-48,91-109,198-210,245-256; docs/SELF_UPDATE.md:59-80).

Restrict publication credentials to privileged workflows; bind tagged engine provenance to generated artifacts and checksum the final signed archive bytes (.github/workflows/release.yml:19-21,230-235,252-321; scripts/release.sh:872-899).
assumptions: No user deployment context, preexisting model or knowledge base was supplied. No production web service, network-accessible MCP transport, multi-tenant hosting, authentication service or container/mount layout is established. The observed MCP startup uses stdio (jubarte-python/python/jubarte_redlines/mcp_server.py:373-381).
Process memory/CPU limits and isolation remain embedding-host obligations; configured archive/XML budgets are not a proof against all denial of service (SECURITY.md:70-74).

The Rust library overview says operations use no temp files, but native font discovery can write font-index.tsv and a sibling font-index.tsv.<pid>.tmp through ambient std::fs. This is font metadata state rather than extracted document parts; applicability requires a rendering path that performs indexed font lookup and a usable configured/default path (src/lib.rs:7-11; src/convert/font.rs:3090-3107,3213-3229).

MCP documentation promises paths under the server root; document path arguments are capability-confined, while native rendering's host-configured font/cache accesses are independent ambient resources. No evidence establishes that an MCP client can change their configuration (jubarte-python/python/jubarte_redlines/mcp_server.py:7-9,67-108; src/convert/font.rs:2633-2652,3098-3107).

The Python/Node adapters advertise shared command behavior, but their general filesystem write helpers differ from native staged publication. Semantic-plan atomicity does not establish cross-adapter multi-file filesystem atomicity (jubarte-python/python/jubarte_redlines/__main__.py:5-7,126-133; jubarte-wasm/cli/bin/jubarte-redlines.mjs:6-8,106-111; src/publication.rs:168-174).

Current signing is explicitly staged: RELEASE_KEYS=[] and FIRST_SIGNED_RELEASE=None match documentation's checksum-only initial phase. Whether deployed older/newer binaries or GitHub secrets differ cannot be determined offline (src/update.rs:29-48; docs/SELF_UPDATE.md:67-80; .github/workflows/release.yml:252-275).

SECURITY.md still describes rdocx-opc 0.2, while the inspected Cargo.toml configures oxml-opc 0.14.2 and two quick-xml versions for distinct consumers. Preserve this documentation/dependency-name disagreement for dependency investigation; it does not by itself establish an exploitable issue (SECURITY.md:87-94; Cargo.toml:102-117).
This pass inspected architecture consumers and source anchors only. It did not execute the application, test controls, inspect live credentials/services or complete a vulnerability audit.

Verified effective native font index: explicit JUBARTE_FONT_INDEX wins; empty/off disables. Otherwise user_font_dir().parent()/font-index.tsv yields macOS $HOME/Library/Application Support/jubarte/font-index.tsv, Linux $XDG_DATA_HOME/jubarte/font-index.tsv or $HOME/.local/share/jubarte/font-index.tsv, Windows %APPDATA%/jubarte/font-index.tsv. Explicit JUBARTE_FONT_DIR maps index to its parent, not inside the font directory. PID sibling staging uses host filesystem authority (src/convert/font.rs:2633-2652,3100-3107,3213-3229).

Verified effective release resources: zipsign private-key reference secrets.ZIPSIGN_PRIVATE_KEY is decoded under $RUNNER_TEMP/zipsign.<random>/key<n>, cleaned on EXIT, and used only in signing step before dist/* SHA256SUMS; GitHub release job uses secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN with contents:write; operator registry clients consume CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN, npm login/NPM_OTP and UV_PUBLISH_TOKEN. Provisioning, runner isolation and registry accounts are external unknowns (.github/workflows/release.yml:252-321,356-369; scripts/release.sh:370-380,655-656,872-899,919-959,1069-1097).

findings.title: Untrusted DOCX table spans cause disproportionate memory allocation
findings.summary: The renderer accepts gridSpan, gridBefore and gridAfter as unbounded usize counts and expands a dense column vector to the summed occupancy. A small admitted DOCX table can request billions of f32 columns, exhausting the host process or triggering a capacity panic before rendering finishes.

severity.rationale: A document supplier can deny availability to a process rendering their document with a tiny numeric payload. Reachability through the public renderer is direct; process resource limits recommended by SECURITY.md reduce blast radius. No remote service deployment or code execution is assumed.
severity.changeConditions: Dedicated per-job process limits reduce impact; a shared long-lived rendering service would increase impact.

confidence.rationale: Independent static trace confirms unchecked span parsing, propagation and dense allocation after admission; no runtime exploit was executed.

codeEvidence.label: Shared renderer admits and then lays out the document
codeEvidence.explanation: Admission enforces package/XML budgets; no layout semantic bound is introduced before DOM use.

codeEvidence.label: Untrusted cell span is parsed without an upper bound
codeEvidence.explanation: The caller-controlled gridSpan value becomes a usize with only a lower bound.

codeEvidence.label: Row skip counts share the unbounded column-count path
codeEvidence.explanation: gridBefore and gridAfter accept any positive usize.

codeEvidence.label: Expanded occupancy controls dense column allocation
codeEvidence.explanation: The sum of spans determines Vec<f32> length, allowing billions of elements from a few input digits.

codeEvidence.label: Body table reaches table_block
codeEvidence.explanation: Body layout dispatches table input to the vulnerable table parser.

rootCause.summary: Table column occupancy is derived directly from document-provided span and skip counts without a semantic ceiling or checked aggregate budget before Vec allocation.

findings.remediation: Apply a finite table-column budget to every gridSpan/gridBefore/gridAfter and their aggregate using checked arithmetic before allocating or iterating expanded column structures; return a typed input refusal.

counterEvidence: SECURITY.md requires host CPU/memory limits and does not promise all DoS prevention.
Existing XML/package limits bound input bytes but not the expanded column count.
This is a rendering availability issue; ordinary read/edit flows without layout are not asserted affected.
limitations: No application code or vulnerability-triggering input executed.
validation.summary: Confirmed render -> with_layout -> body table_block -> cell_span/row_grid_skip -> RawCell.colspan -> occupancy -> Vec allocation. Admission checks archive sizes, XML depth and tag widths, not these numeric layout counts.

dataflow.summary: DOCX table attribute -> parsed usize -> RawCell.colspan -> summed row occupancy -> vec!/resize of columns

impact.why: Rendering host process can exhaust memory or abort/panic.

likelihood.why: A small attacker-controlled integer reaches allocation through normal rendering.

reachability.summary: Public render and PDF/PNG/report wrappers invoke with_layout on caller-supplied DOCX bytes. A single visible table row suffices; no nondefault option is required.
reachability.attacker: supplier of document bytes rendered by another process
preconditions: Victim renders attacker-supplied DOCX; impact is constrained by host process limits.

attackPath.summary: A supplier provides a compact DOCX table with an extreme positive span/skip value. A victim renders it through the library or a binding and allocates a column vector sized by that value.

remediationTests: Integration-test huge cell spans and row skips through public rendering APIs and assert bounded typed refusal, including aggregate overflow.
Keep representative valid merged tables rendering correctly within the budget.

findings.title: Unbounded DOCX numbering levels cause CPU and memory exhaustion
findings.summary: Paragraph ilvl and numbering definitions accept arbitrary u32 values. Missing-level fallback scans the entire numeric range, while an explicitly defined huge level inserts counters for all lower levels. Compact document attributes can induce billions of operations or allocations during normal rendering.

severity.rationale: A document supplier can deny availability to the renderer process with a small input. Impact is availability and the direct normal parsing path is highly reachable; no public hosting assumption is needed. Host process limits bound collateral impact.
severity.changeConditions: Dedicated worker CPU/memory limits reduce impact; a shared rendering process would increase impact.

confidence.rationale: Independent source trace confirms unbounded level parsing and both range-sized sinks after package admission; runtime reproduction was not performed.

codeEvidence.label: Paragraph numbering level accepts arbitrary u32
codeEvidence.explanation: Paragraph numbering level accepts arbitrary u32; no semantic 0..8 ceiling is applied.

rootCause.summary: Semantic numbering-level identifiers are accepted as unrestricted u32 values and reused as numeric iteration bounds instead of being validated or looked up among actual defined levels.

findings.remediation: Validate paragraph/style/abstract/override ilvl values against supported levels before use; locate fallback parents among defined keys and avoid any work proportional to an untrusted numeric level.

counterEvidence: Admission limits XML/container bytes and tag policy, not numbering schema values.
No issue is asserted for bounded ordinary levels.
limitations: No application execution or exploit-input creation.
validation.summary: Verified num_pr -> list_marker -> next_revised/next_marker -> resolve_ilvl. A request for u32::MAX with only level 0 defined causes about 4.3 billion reverse lookups. Defining a huge level bypasses that search but reaches lower-counter materialization for every level.

dataflow.summary: w:ilvl/@w:val and numbering definitions -> parsed u32 -> list_marker -> next_marker -> reverse range search or per-level counter insertion
dataflow.sink: range-sized hash lookups and counter allocation

likelihood.why: Short numeric input directly controls normal layout work.

reachability.summary: Caller-controlled document bytes enter public rendering/layout APIs through with_layout and admission; ordinary numbering on one paragraph reaches the affected routines.
reachability.attacker: supplier of a DOCX rendered by a victim
preconditions: Victim processes untrusted document using layout; no nondefault configuration required.

attackPath.summary: An attacker supplies a DOCX with huge paragraph list level and a normal or matching huge numbering definition; rendering performs work proportional to the numeric value.

remediationTests: Exercise huge paragraph ilvl against level-0 numbering and assert fast typed refusal.
Exercise huge definition/override levels and assert no expanded counter allocation; retain ordinary 0..8 behavior.

originalCandidates.title: Unbounded numbering levels drive CPU or memory exhaustion
originalCandidates.evidence: Untrusted paragraph w:numPr/w:ilvl/@w:val parsed u32 without 0..8 bound at src/convert/mod.rs:12711-12714. Numbering::resolve_ilvl at 5529-5531 scans (0..ilvl).rev().find(lvls.contains_key), so ilvl=4294967295 against ordinary level-0 definition burns ~4.3 billion hash probes. Defining huge level itself (parsed unchecked at 6619-6622) instead reaches next_marker 5610-5630, inserting a counter/string for every lower level, exhausting memory. list_marker 12879 invokes next_revised. No schema validation in convert::with_layout: admit_package checks XML/container, not numbering semantics.

findings.title: Python and Node plan recording follow attacker-planted temporary symlinks
findings.summary: Both CLI adapters stage a recorded plan in .<plan>.<pid>.partial using a nonexclusive create/truncate write. A local attacker able to create entries beside the selected plan can plant that predictable name as a symlink and cause the victim to overwrite another victim-writable file with plan JSON.

severity.rationale: Arbitrary victim-writable file corruption crosses an OS-user boundary, but requires a shared writable plan directory and predicting or observing the victim PID. The local, constrained prerequisites lower likelihood; document-only attackers cannot exploit this.
severity.changeConditions: Private output directories prevent the prerequisite; a privileged victim writing plans in an untrusted shared directory increases impact.

confidence.rationale: Independent source trace confirms both adapters open predictable partial names with ordinary truncating writes before rename; no exclusive open or nofollow guard is present.

codeEvidence.label: Native recorder already uses hardened publication
codeEvidence.explanation: Native recorder already uses hardened publication

rootCause.summary: Plan recording independently reimplements filesystem publication in Python and Node with PID-only temporary names and nonexclusive truncation, bypassing the native recorder's private staging controls.

findings.remediation: Have Python and Node plan recording use exclusive private random staging, as the native publication backend does. Never truncate an existing temporary entry; stage a regular file in a held trusted parent and atomically replace only the authorized plan.

counterEvidence: Dry-run and failed preview skip publication.

findings.title: Nested legacy DOC field results cause quadratic parsing work
findings.summary: The legacy DOC parser scans the entire field-state stack for every story character. Repeated nested field starts followed by separators leave a growing stack of false entries, forcing quadratic work on otherwise bounded text input.

severity.rationale: An untrusted legacy document can consume disproportionate CPU through the public conversion parser. Impact is availability and normal conversion is directly reachable; external process limits reduce blast radius.
severity.changeConditions: CPU-limited isolated jobs reduce impact; a shared long-lived converter increases impact.

confidence.rationale: Independent static source trace confirms attacker influence, reachable sink and missing control. No application code or exploit inputs were executed.

rootCause.summary: Story::blocks recomputes whether any field is in its code phase by scanning all nested field flags on each character, with no nesting/work limit or constant-time aggregate state.

findings.remediation: Maintain a constant-time count of open code-phase fields and update it on field transitions, and enforce a finite field nesting/work budget.

counterEvidence: Compound-file sector and stream bounds prevent out-of-range reads but do not bound field-stack work.
This affects legacy DOC parsing, not all DOCX paths.
limitations: Offline static analysis only; no runtime reproduction or deployment verification.
validation.summary: Verified public read decodes piece-table text to StoryChar values and calls Story::blocks; compressed and UTF-16 decoders preserve field control characters. Each start/separator pair grows an all-false stack, so iter().any scans a progressively larger prefix. No field-depth cap intervenes in the inspected path.

dataflow.summary: WordDocument piece-table character bytes -> StoryChar -> Story::blocks -> fields.iter().any per character

impact.why: Excess CPU consumption can monopolize a conversion worker.

likelihood.why: The parser preserves the relevant field characters and does not constrain field depth.

reachability.summary: Public legacy_doc::read, doc_to_markdown and doc_to_docx invoke the affected parser; CLI legacy conversion also calls doc_to_docx.
reachability.attacker: supplier of a legacy DOC processed by another user/application

attackPath.summary: A supplier nests many legacy DOC fields in result state; a victim converting the document repeatedly scans the accumulated field stack and spends quadratic CPU.

remediationTests: Use a deterministic parser test with many nested result-phase fields; assert bounded work using an instrumented operation count and correct ordinary field output.
